title: Greater than and less than
subtitle: Compare numbers and put them in order.

explanation.title: The wide side of the sign

questions.prompt: Mia writes −3 < −9. What has she done wrong?
options: The wide side should face −3, because −3 is bigger.
Nothing. Her sign is right.
She should have written −3 = −9.
The bigger number always goes second.
feedback: Yes. −3 > −9, because −3 is further right on the number line.
−3 < −9 says −3 is less than −9. But −9 is further left on the number line, so −9 is smaller.
= means both sides are the same. −3 and −9 aren't the same.
Either order works: −3 > −9 and −9 < −3 are both right. It's the sign that's wrong.

questions.prompt: Ben says 0.35 is bigger than 0.4 because it has more digits. Is he right?
options: No. 0.4 = 0.40, and 40 hundredths is more than 35 hundredths.
Yes. More digits means a bigger number.
Yes, because 35 is bigger than 4.
No. They're the same size.
feedback: Yes. Add a zero so both have the same number of digits, then compare.
Not after the decimal point. 4 tenths is more than 3 tenths.
The 35 and the 4 aren't in the same places. Write 0.4 as 0.40, then compare 40 with 35.
0.4 = 0.40. 40 hundredths and 35 hundredths aren't the same.

questions.prompt: A pen costs £3.05 and a pencil case costs £3.50. Which sentence is true?
options: The pen is cheaper, because 0 tenths is less than 5 tenths.
The pencil case is cheaper, because 3.50 has a 0 at the end.
They cost the same, because they use the same digits.
The pen costs more, because it ends in a 5.
feedback: Yes. Both start with £3, so look at the tenths next.
A 0 at the end doesn't make a number smaller. £3.50 is the same as £3.5.
The digits are in different places. 5 tenths is worth more than 5 hundredths.
Look at the first place where the prices are different, not the last digit.

questions.prompt: A balance scale tips down on the left. What does that tell you?
options: The left side is heavier, so left > right.
The left side is lighter, so left < right.
Both sides weigh the same, so left = right.
The right side is heavier, so right > left.
feedback: Yes. The heavier side goes down.
The lighter side goes up, not down.
If they weighed the same, the scale would be level.
The right side went up, so it's the lighter side.

options: −100, because it's further left on the number line.
0, because 100 is bigger than 0.
0, because nothing is less than 0.
They're the same, because 0 and −100 both end in 0.
feedback: Yes. Every number below zero is less than 0, however big it looks.
The minus sign matters. −100 is 100 below zero.
Every negative number is less than 0.
Ending in 0 doesn't make two numbers the same. −100 is 100 below zero.

points.text: The wide side of the sign faces the bigger number.
Add zeros at the end of a decimal to help you compare.
Compare pounds first, then tenths, then hundredths.
On a balance scale, the heavier side goes down.
The further left a number is on a number line, the smaller it is.
